goal: Notice when you've only followed one link of a chain
script: Before you finish — how confident are you that you've traced every connection, not just the first one? What made you stop looking: ran out of ideas, or unsure how to check?
why: The second question isn't about food webs at all. It asks students to inspect their own reasoning for completeness — a monitoring move they can reuse on any 'what happens if…' problem.
evidence: Self-questioning to probe understanding — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Name systems thinking as a learnable, transferable habit
script: Today isn't only about ecosystems — we're practising systems thinking: deliberately looking for effects more than one step away. You'll use this in geography and in life, not just here.
why: Posting the thinking intention beside the content intention makes the strategy visible, which the guide identifies as what helps a strategy transfer beyond the lesson it was learned in.
evidence: 'Be explicit' about strategies, not just content — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Plan a reasoning approach before diving in
script: Before your prediction, set up two columns: direct effects, and indirect effects one step removed. What's your plan for not stopping at the first effect?
why: A graphic organiser used before the task is a classic planning strategy; here it externalises the very step (looking past the obvious) students usually skip.
evidence: Planning strategies incl. graphic organisers — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Make the 'getting stuck and re-checking' moment visible
script: Remove the small fish… algae grows… wait — that also changes what the big fish eat. I need to go back and re-check that branch.
why: Thinking aloud through an unfamiliar web, and pausing audibly at 'wait', gives students a script for their own internal monologue when a prediction unravels.
evidence: Think-aloud modelling; Predict–Observe–Explain revision — White & Frederiksen (1998).

goal: Self-test whether first-instinct reasoning holds
script: Here's a web where the obvious answer is wrong — a species that looks minor but props up three others. Write your first instinct, then look again. Did anything change your mind?
why: Introducing a non-obvious keystone species once basic chains are secure forces students to test their own model against a counter-example rather than pattern-match.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks once confident — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Grade your reasoning, not just the science answer
script: Two lines to rate yourself: 'I can identify producers, consumers, decomposers' — and separately — 'I checked for indirect effects before I finished.'
why: Most students have never been asked to grade the second kind of statement. Splitting content-mastery from thinking-process is the heart of the evaluate phase.
evidence: Evaluating: self-testing of the process — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: See that others reason differently on the same web
script: Compare predictions in your group. Did anyone check something you didn't? Not who's right — whose method was different from yours?
why: Social metacognition: students learn about their own thinking by seeing an unfamiliar strategy enacted by a peer, then can adopt it.
evidence: Social metacognition in group work — CBE–LSE evidence guide (2021).

goal: Build a reusable habit of checking indirect effects
script: Grassland last week, rainforest today, a coral reef on Friday — same two-column check each time. The system changes; the thinking move stays the same.
why: Reusing one routine across varied content (interleaving) is what turns a one-off worksheet into a durable, transferable habit.
evidence: Interleaving & distributed practice — CBE–LSE evidence guide (2021).

goal: Check whether the habit is becoming automatic
script: When you saw a brand-new web today, did you automatically look for indirect effects, or did you have to remind yourself?
why: The shift from reminded to automatic is your real evidence the habit is forming — more informative than any single quiz mark.
evidence: Assessing metacognition during task performance — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Question whether a sample really represents the whole
script: Before you scale up your quadrat count — ask yourself: is the patch I sampled typical of the whole oval, or did I pick the easy spot?
why: Turns an unspoken shortcut (sampling convenient ground) into a conscious check students perform on their own method.

goal: Name 'checking representativeness' as a skill for life
script: The thing we're really practising is judging whether a sample represents a bigger group — you'll meet this in every poll, survey and news headline you ever read.
why: Explicitly framing sampling as a general reasoning habit lifts it above this one fieldwork lesson.

goal: Decide the checks before collecting data
script: On your planning sheet, write the two questions you'll ask of your own results: is my sample big enough, and is it placed fairly?
why: Front-loading the monitoring questions means students judge their method as they work, not only when results look odd.
evidence: Investigation planning sheet — NSW DoE science resources.

goal: Show the moment of doubting your own data
script: My first three quadrats all landed on bare dirt — that's making me doubt my placement was random. Let me talk through how I'd fix that before I trust these numbers.
why: Modelling productive doubt about one's own data normalises revision instead of pushing on with a flawed sample.

goal: Transfer the method to a messier site
script: Now design a sample for a site with a creek down one side. The even-grid plan won't work — talk me through what you'll change and why.
why: A site that breaks the default method tests whether students' planning survives without the scaffold.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Reflect on the method, separately from the result
script: Two-part reflection: what did your data show, and — separately — how much do you trust your own sampling, and why?
why: Splitting 'what I found' from 'how good my method was' builds the habit of evaluating the process.
evidence: Student reflection on investigations — NSW DoE science resources.

goal: Compare sampling choices across groups
script: Each group used the same oval but different placements. Whose sample do you trust most, and what does that tell you about your own choice?
why: Comparing methods surfaces trade-offs no single group would notice alone.

goal: Reuse the representativeness check across contexts
script: Same two questions — big enough? placed fairly? — when we survey the schoolyard, then a data set I hand you, then a news poll.
why: Repeating one check across very different data sources makes the habit content-independent.

goal: Check whether the check has become automatic
script: Without me prompting — what's the first thing you now ask when someone shows you a survey result?
why: An unprompted reflex is the evidence the monitoring habit has taken hold.
evidence: Assessing metacognition in performance — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Surface the mental picture behind an answer
script: You said the puck keeps moving — in your head just then, was something still pushing it, or nothing? Describe the picture, not the rule.
why: Targets the image a student is using, where the misconception actually lives, rather than the memorised rule.
evidence: Self-questioning to reveal misconceptions — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Name the exact misconception being replaced
script: Almost everyone starts out believing motion needs a constant push. That specific idea is what we're rebuilding today — watch for it in your own thinking.
why: Naming the misconception gives students a concrete thing to catch themselves doing.

goal: Plan a force-diagram routine before predicting
script: Before you predict, draw every force as an arrow, then decide if they cancel. Predict the motion only after the diagram, never before.
why: A fixed 'diagram-first' sequence stops students answering from intuition and then rationalising.
evidence: Planning strategies incl. diagrams — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Show catching your own wrong intuition
script: My gut says it slows because nothing's pushing… but my diagram shows zero net force. My gut's wrong here — the diagram wins. Let me say why.
why: Modelling the teacher's own intuition being overruled by evidence is powerful permission for students to do the same.

goal: Test the idea in a frictionless/space context
script: Now the same puck in deep space, no friction. Predict, then tell me which part of your reasoning you were least sure about.
why: A context that strips away friction tests whether the corrected model holds, and naming uncertainty is itself a monitoring act.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Separate 'I can define it' from 'I still picture it wrong'
script: Rate two things: 'I can state Newton's first law' and, honestly, 'I still sometimes picture motion as needing a push.'
why: The second line targets the misconception directly, which recall of the definition can hide.

goal: Compare force diagrams and reasoning aloud
script: Compare arrows with your partner. Where you disagree, whoever explains their diagram out loud is the one who learns the most — so take turns.
why: Explaining a diagram aloud is self-explanation; disagreement forces both partners to check their own reasoning.

goal: Rehearse diagram-first across many scenarios
script: Trolley, lift, falling coffee filter, hockey puck — every one starts with the force diagram. The scenario changes; the routine doesn't.
why: Repeating the routine across varied scenarios makes 'diagram first' automatic rather than reminded.

goal: Check whether the misconception has gone quiet or gone
script: Be honest — if you had to bet, is any part of you still tempted by 'moving means something's pushing'?
why: Misconceptions often go underground rather than disappearing; a direct check surfaces them while there's time to act.
evidence: Monitoring misconceptions over time — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Ask what a surprising point means before explaining it
script: That point breaks the trend. Before you explain it away — ask yourself: is this telling me something real, or is it a measurement slip? How would you tell the difference?
why: Converts the reflex to 'smooth over' anomalies into a deliberate monitoring question.
evidence: Self-questioning; monitoring surprising data — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Name 'reading data critically' as the day's thinking goal
script: The science is the graph. The thinking skill is not taking a data point at face value — that's what we're really building.
why: Distinguishes the content (this graph) from the transferable habit (scepticism about data).

goal: Set the questions you'll ask of any graph
script: Write your three-question graph routine now: what's the overall trend, does any point break it, and what could explain that?
why: A pre-set reading routine means students arrive at a graph with a plan rather than staring at it.

goal: Think aloud reading a graph, including the stuck moment
script: First the overall trend… hmm, this point doesn't fit. I'm stuck — so I check the units, then I check if it's a single reading or an average.
why: Naming the stuck moment and the recovery strategy gives students a template for their own.

goal: Give a graph where the anomaly IS the finding
script: Here's one where the odd point is the whole story, not an error. Does your usual 'ignore the outlier' instinct serve you here?
why: Breaking the default rule tests whether students are thinking or applying a script.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Rate your interpretation process
script: Did you decide about the anomaly on evidence, or on a gut 'that looks wrong'? Rate your own process, not just your conclusion.
why: Focuses evaluation on how the judgement was made.

goal: Compare verdicts on the same anomaly
script: Same graph, compare verdicts. What did someone else notice about that point that you missed?
why: Peers surface features and interpretations an individual misses.

goal: Reuse the three-question routine on new graphs
script: New data set each lesson, same three questions. The topic changes; your reading routine gets stronger.
why: Repetition across content builds a durable reading habit.

goal: Check for unprompted critical reading
script: Has anyone caught themselves questioning a graph in an ad or on social media this week?
why: Self-reported transfer outside class is strong evidence the habit has stuck.
evidence: Assessing metacognition in natural settings — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Turn variable-control into a self-check
script: Before you submit this method, answer three questions in writing: what am I changing, what am I measuring, and what am I keeping the same?
why: Students can define 'variable' on a test yet never turn it into a question about their own plan. This routine forces that.

goal: Name fair-test design as a habit for every prac
script: These three questions aren't for this experiment — they're for every practical this year and your depth study. The topic changes; the questions don't.
why: Frames the routine as transferable disciplinary method, not a one-off.

goal: Use one reusable planning scaffold
script: Same planning template every time: question, variables, method, controls, safety, expected pattern. Its familiarity is the point.
why: A content-free scaffold reused all year is what carries the metacognitive value.
evidence: Investigation planning sheet — NSW DoE science resources.

goal: Think aloud spotting your own uncontrolled variable
script: I said I'm testing surface type… but I swabbed the door at lunch and the desk at 9am. Time is now a second variable I didn't control. Let me fix that.
why: Modelling the catch, not just the corrected method, teaches the monitoring move.

goal: Design for an open question with no obvious variable
script: Now an open question with no single obvious variable to change. Rebuild the three planning questions from memory — no template this time.
why: Removing the scaffold tests whether the routine has been internalised.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Self-mark the plan before results arrive
script: Before you run it, self-check: did I identify all three variable types? Is it genuinely a fair test? Mark your plan, then I'll mark it.
why: Judging the plan before results keeps the reflection about method, not about whether it 'worked'.
evidence: Self-assessment; evaluating the process — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Peer-review draft methods
script: Swap plans. Each partner finds one thing the writer missed using the three questions. Notice which question you keep forgetting.
why: Peers catch different gaps; noticing your own blind spot is metacognitive knowledge.

goal: Withdraw the scaffold over the year
script: By mid-year I want those three questions coming from you, not the template. We'll track how much scaffold you still need.
why: Visible fading of support is the goal, not a new skill each time.
evidence: Gradual release; distributed practice — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Check for the routine as a default
script: Without me saying anything — what are your first three questions when you start planning any investigation?
why: Reciting the routine unprompted is evidence it's a habit, not compliance.
evidence: Assessing metacognition in performance — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Ask why a claim feels convincing before asking if it's true
script: What about this source made you want to believe it — and is that a good scientific reason?
why: Separates a persuasive source from a reliable one, and turns inspection back onto the student's own reaction.

goal: Name 'evidence quality' as the transferable target
script: We're building one skill: noticing when a claim outruns its evidence. This is for every health headline you'll ever read, not just this one.
why: Makes the habit, not the example, the point.

goal: Fix your criteria before reading either source
script: Before you read, write the questions you'll ask of each source — sample size, who funded it, has it been repeated — so the content can't sway your standards.
why: Setting criteria first guards against being persuaded and then rationalising.

goal: Narrate nearly being persuaded too fast
script: 'A study found…' — that sounds solid… wait, it doesn't say how many people. I nearly accepted that. Let me find the sample size first.
why: The near-miss, modelled aloud, is the behaviour worth copying.
evidence: Think-aloud; evaluating scientific data — NSW DoE resources.

goal: Test evenhandedness against a disliked conclusion
script: Here's a well-evidenced claim that cuts against what most of us assume. Are you using the same evidence standard as before, or is this one harder to accept?
why: Reveals motivated reasoning — a hard, high-value monitoring skill.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Check your verdict against your own criteria
script: Go back to the questions you planned. Did you actually use each one, or fall back on gut feeling under time pressure?
why: Evaluates the process against the student's own stated standard.

goal: Compare verdicts on identical evidence
script: Same source, compare verdicts. People can weigh identical evidence differently — what did your group weigh more heavily than you did?
why: Shows evaluation is a judgement with visible reasoning, not a lookup.

goal: Rehearse across health, climate, tech claims
script: Different topic every time — vaccine, diet, phone radiation — same evaluative questions. You're building the habit, not becoming an expert in one topic.
why: Varying content isolates the transferable skill.

goal: Check for transfer beyond the classroom
script: Anyone catch themselves asking these questions about something on their feed this week?
why: Out-of-class transfer is the strongest evidence the habit is real.
evidence: Assessing metacognition in natural settings — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Probe where the 'missing' mass went
script: You said mass was lost when the candle burned. Where exactly did it go — and how could we check whether it's really gone or just moved?
why: Turns a stated misconception into an investigable question the student poses to themselves.
evidence: Self-questioning to surface misconceptions — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Name the 'mass can hide as gas' idea directly
script: The trap today is thinking mass disappears when we can't see it. That exact idea is what we're testing and replacing.
why: Gives students the misconception by name so they can catch it in themselves.

goal: Predict-then-weigh as a planned routine
script: Predict the mass change in writing and why, before you weigh anything. We're checking your reasoning against the balance.
why: Committing a reasoned prediction first is Predict–Observe–Explain: the mismatch becomes data about thinking.

goal: Show revising a belief when the balance disagrees
script: I expected the sealed flask to get lighter… it didn't. So my 'gas escapes = mass lost' idea can't be right when nothing escapes. Let me rebuild it.
why: Modelling belief revision in response to evidence is the target thinking move.

goal: Apply it to an open vs sealed system
script: Same reaction, once sealed and once open. Predict both, then say which prediction you trust less and why.
why: The open/closed contrast tests whether the corrected model generalises; naming lower confidence is a monitoring act.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Separate stating the law from believing it
script: Rate both: 'I can state that mass is conserved' and 'I honestly still expect burning things to lose mass.'
why: The second line targets the surviving misconception the definition can mask.

goal: Reconcile conflicting predictions in pairs
script: You predicted lighter, your partner predicted the same — the balance says no change. Talk out where your shared reasoning went wrong.
why: Explaining a wrong shared prediction aloud is high-value self-explanation.

goal: Reuse predict-then-weigh across reactions
script: Precipitation, effervescence, combustion — predict the mass change and reason first, every time.
why: Repetition builds the predict-first habit across reaction types.

goal: Check whether the misconception resurfaces
script: New reaction, no warning — what does your gut say about the mass, and do you still trust it?
why: An unprompted check reveals whether the old idea has truly gone.
evidence: Monitoring misconceptions over time — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Distinguish a probability from a guarantee, out loud
script: You wrote '3 will be tall'. Ask yourself: does the square predict exactly three, or the probability of each? What's the difference for a litter of four?
why: Forces students to inspect whether they're reasoning in probabilities or slipping into certainties.

goal: Name probabilistic reasoning as the real skill
script: The genetics is the cross. The thinking skill is reading a ratio as a probability, not a promise — and that trips people up in stats and risk everywhere.
why: Lifts the transferable reasoning above the specific cross.

goal: Fix a genotype-then-phenotype sequence
script: Plan the steps before you fill anything in: parental genotypes, gametes, grid, genotype ratio, then phenotype ratio. Don't jump to phenotype.
why: A planned sequence prevents the common genotype/phenotype conflation.

goal: Show catching a genotype/phenotype slip
script: I've got 1:2:1 genotypes… wait, the question asked phenotype, that's 3:1. I nearly answered the wrong ratio — always re-read which one they want.
why: Modelling the self-catch teaches the checking move directly.

goal: Move to a dihybrid or linked-gene case
script: Now two genes at once. Predict, then tell me which step you're least confident about before you commit.
why: A harder cross tests whether the routine transfers; naming the shaky step is monitoring.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Grade reasoning, not just the ratio
script: Did you get 3:1 by understanding, or by copying the pattern from last question? Rate how well you understood, separately from the answer.
why: Separates a correct answer from secure reasoning.

goal: Explain a cross to a partner as a check
script: Explain your cross to your partner using only 'because'. If you can't finish a 'because', that's exactly where to look again.
why: Self-explanation exposes gaps a correct grid can hide.

goal: Interleave inheritance types
script: Mix them deliberately — autosomal, sex-linked, codominant — in one set, so you have to decide the type, not just apply one.
why: Interleaving forces discrimination between problem types, which blocked practice hides.

goal: Check the re-read habit is automatic
script: Quick show of hands — who now automatically re-reads whether a question wants genotype or phenotype?
why: An automatic re-read reflex is the sign the habit has formed.
evidence: Assessing metacognition in performance — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Interrogate the verb before writing
script: Before you write — what is 'assess' actually asking you to do here, and how is that different from 'describe'? Answer that first.
why: Unpacking the directive verb is a planning-level monitoring move most students skip.
evidence: Self-questioning; scientific thinking scaffold — NSW DoE resources.

goal: Name criteria-reading as a transferable skill
script: We're practising turning marking criteria into a checklist you write against — a skill for every extended response and your depth study report.
why: Frames exam technique as a durable self-regulation habit.

goal: Translate the criteria into self-questions first
script: Turn the marking rubric into three questions in your own words — e.g. 'have I linked innate and adaptive, not just listed them?' — and plan against those.
why: Generating the questions themselves forces students to internalise the standard.
evidence: Planning; exam wrappers — self-regulated learning research.

goal: Think aloud drafting against the criteria
script: The rubric wants 'links between components'. My first sentence just lists them — that's a 'describe', not 'assess'. Let me add the link I'm missing.
why: Modelling the criteria-check mid-draft shows monitoring in action.

goal: Apply to an unfamiliar cross-module prompt
script: Here's a question blending immunity and non-infectious disease. Which criteria still apply, and which parts of your plan need changing?
why: A novel synthesis prompt tests whether the criteria-routine transfers.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks; cross-module — NSW DoE resources.

goal: Self-mark before the teacher marks
script: Mark your own draft against the rubric first — annotate where you think you did and didn't meet each criterion. Then compare with my marking.
why: The gap between self-mark and teacher-mark becomes the feedback conversation.

goal: Peer-mark using the same rubric
script: Swap responses and mark each other with the rubric. Where you and your partner disagree on a mark, that's the criterion to discuss.
why: Peer-marking builds shared understanding of the standard.

goal: Repeat criteria-first across modules
script: Every extended response this term starts by turning the criteria into your own questions — immunity now, homeostasis next.
why: Repetition across modules builds a durable writing routine.

goal: Check whether criteria-reading is now automatic
script: Before assessment week — do you now read the rubric before you start writing, without me telling you?
why: An unprompted rubric-first habit is the evidence sought.

goal: Check which mental picture is really in play
script: When you pictured equilibrium just then — was anything still moving, or had it gone still? Describe the picture, not the definition.
why: Students can give textbook wording while still picturing a static system; the question targets the picture.
evidence: Self-questioning to surface misconceptions — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Name the 'stopped' misconception directly
script: Almost everyone starts by picturing equilibrium as stopped. That specific idea is what we're replacing today — not adding on top of.
why: Naming it gives students a concrete thing to catch in their own thinking.

goal: Use a deliberate three-step Le Châtelier check
script: Fix the sequence before answering: what's the stress, which direction relieves it, and does that match my first guess?
why: Planning the steps catches a wrong instinct instead of locking it in.

goal: Show a conceptual check differs from a calculation check
script: For the Kc calculation I'm checking units and my ICE table. For this shift question I'm checking my mental model — a totally different kind of mistake to look for.
why: Naming the difference stops quantitative habits leaking into conceptual reasoning.

goal: Predict for two simultaneous stresses
script: Two stresses at once now. Predict, then name the part of your reasoning you're least sure of.
why: A multi-variable case tests robustness; naming uncertainty is diagnostic.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Separate defining from truly picturing it
script: Rate two lines: 'I can define dynamic equilibrium' and 'if I'm honest, I still sometimes picture it as stopped.'
why: The second line targets the actual misconception, not recall.

goal: Explain a predicted shift to a partner
script: Explain your shift to your partner using only 'the system responds by…'. Can't finish it without 'it just goes that way'? Then it's not secure yet.
why: Self-explanation reveals whether reasoning is genuine.

goal: Reuse the three-step check across reactions
script: Stress / direction / match-my-instinct — same check on Haber, on esterification, on a solubility equilibrium.
why: Repetition across systems makes the check automatic.

goal: Check the misconception is gone, not just quiet
script: A few lessons from assessment — if you had to bet, is any part of you still tempted by 'equilibrium means stopped'?
why: Misconceptions go underground; a direct check surfaces them in time.
evidence: Monitoring misconceptions over time — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Build a running sense-check into the working
script: At each line, ask: are my units still consistent, and is this number a sensible size for a titration? Don't wait until the end.
why: Converts silent calculation into monitored calculation.

goal: Name self-monitoring as the calculation skill
script: The chemistry is the stoichiometry. The thinking skill is catching your own slip before the final line — that's what separates reliable problem-solvers.
why: Makes the monitoring habit, not just the maths, explicit.

goal: Use a four-stage problem card
script: Understand, plan, solve, check — name what each line is doing before you write it. What's given, what's asked, which relationship links them?
why: A staged card externalises the planning most students do implicitly (or skip).
evidence: Planning strategies incl. checklists — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Think aloud through a stuck point
script: I've got moles of acid but the question wants concentration of base… I'm stuck. So I go back to the balanced equation for the mole ratio.
why: Naming the stuck point and the recovery strategy gives students a template.

goal: Give a problem with a distractor number
script: This one has an extra value you don't need. Which of your four stages catches that — and did it?
why: A distractor tests whether students are monitoring, not just plugging numbers.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Reflect on which stage you skipped
script: Which of understand-plan-solve-check did you rush or skip today? That's usually where the error is.
why: Evaluating one's own process pinpoints the habit to strengthen.

goal: Trade error-spotting on worked solutions
script: Swap solutions and find each other's slip using the four stages. Which stage does your partner skip that you don't?
why: Peers reveal characteristic error patterns.

goal: Retire the card as it internalises
script: Once the four stages are automatic, I stop giving the card — you just ask 'which stage am I in?' The scaffold fades, the habit stays.
why: Deliberate scaffold withdrawal is the aim.
evidence: Gradual release; distributed practice — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Check the sense-check is automatic
script: Without prompting — what's the last thing you now do before writing a final answer?
why: An unprompted final sense-check is the evidence the habit holds.

goal: Test whether the two components are being kept separate
script: You said the faster ball hits later. Ask yourself: what decides the fall time — the horizontal speed, or only the vertical drop? Which am I actually using?
why: Surfaces whether the student is treating the components as independent, where the misconception lives.

goal: Name component-independence as the key idea to watch
script: The trap is letting horizontal speed leak into your vertical thinking. That's the exact habit of mind we're building resistance to today.
why: Names the misconception so students can self-monitor for it.

goal: Separate-the-axes as a planned first step
script: Before any numbers, split the problem into two columns — horizontal and vertical — and list what's constant in each. Always before, never during.
why: A planned separation stops the components being tangled from the start.

goal: Show catching the components leaking together
script: I'm about to use horizontal speed to find fall time… no — that's the mistake. Fall time comes from vertical only. Let me catch that and reset.
why: Modelling the self-catch is the core teaching move.

goal: Use a launch at an angle
script: Now a launch at 30°, not horizontal. Predict, then say which of your two columns you're less sure about.
why: An angled launch tests whether independence still holds under a harder case.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Separate getting the answer from believing the model
script: Rate: 'I can calculate the range' and 'I honestly still half-expect a faster ball to stay up longer.'
why: The second line targets the surviving intuition the calculation can mask.

goal: Reconcile predictions with the demo
script: Groups predict for the drop-vs-launch demo. When the two balls land together, talk through whose reasoning that surprises and why.
why: The shared surprise, discussed, drives conceptual change.
evidence: Social metacognition; conceptual change — CBE–LSE guide (2021).

goal: Reuse split-the-axes across scenarios
script: Thrown ball, dropped package from a plane, water jet — split the axes first every time.
why: Repetition makes 'separate the components' automatic.

goal: Check the intuition has actually shifted
script: New projectile, no warning — what does your gut say about fall time, and do you trust it yet?
why: An unprompted check reveals whether the misconception has truly gone.
evidence: Monitoring misconceptions over time — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Build in recurring self-directed questions
script: At each checkpoint, ask yourself the same three: is my question still answerable, is my method still working, and what would I change now?
why: Recurring self-questions turn a long project into a monitored one.

goal: Name the study as a metacognition vehicle
script: Your depth study isn't only assessed on findings — it's where you show you can plan, monitor and evaluate your own thinking over weeks. That's the real skill.
why: Makes the self-regulation goal of the task explicit from the start.

goal: Set personal learning goals alongside the question
script: Alongside your research question, write one or two personal goals — e.g. 'get better at spotting confounds' — in your log-book on day one.
why: Personal goals give the evaluate phase something concrete to revisit.

goal: Model a mid-project pivot honestly
script: Here's a study where my first method wasn't giving reliable data, so at week three I changed it — and here's exactly how I reasoned about that pivot.
why: Modelling a real pivot normalises revising a plan mid-stream.

goal: Push toward a genuinely open question
script: Once your method's secure, extend to a sub-question you don't already know the answer to. Where does your confidence drop, and why?
why: A truly open extension tests independent inquiry, the point of a depth study.
evidence: Challenge with novel tasks — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Revisit day-one goals at the end
script: Back to your original goals — did you achieve them? What would you plan differently if you started again? And: what do I think I've learned about how I work?
why: Closing the loop on personal goals is the fullest form of the evaluate phase.
evidence: Evaluating; open-ended reflection prompts — NSW DoE (2020).

goal: Peer-consult at checkpoints
script: At each checkpoint, one peer asks you the three monitoring questions. Hearing how they'd approach it often shows a method you hadn't considered.
why: Peer consultation surfaces alternative strategies.

goal: Keep short, scheduled log entries
script: Two or three sentences at fixed points — not open-ended. The log-book supports the study; it shouldn't become a second assignment.
why: Short, spaced entries build the habit without adding burden.

goal: Check self-regulation is becoming independent
script: By the final weeks — are you running these checks yourself, or still waiting for me to prompt them?
why: Independent self-regulation is the ultimate goal of the depth study.
evidence: Assessing metacognition in performance — NSW DoE (2020).
